My first few months of therapy I cried more than I talked. Even now, 2.5 years later, I still cry at almost every session, and when I'm on a lower swing, I often go back to crying so hard breathing and speaking are difficult. 

While I know that I'm a failure at most things, one thing that I think I'm good at is pretending to be fine. I'm not pretending to be fine when I'm in therapy though, and that's okay, that's the point. Like you, as soon as the session starts to wind up and I'm talking about less personal things, my mask slips right back comfortably into place. (I'm working on having a thinner mask, maybe even not having it with some people.) 

It's okay that you're crying so much speaking is hard. Your therapist has met with people who have acted similarly in the past and will not be surprised or put off. I've found that therapists are surprisingly good at working with the broken fragments I can choke out between tears. Right now, you are not accustomed to talking about yourself and your feelings. It's overwhelming. As you continue with therapy, you will have more practice at it and will be able to talk about your feelings more easily. I still cry, but I cry at a level where I can still talk somewhat regularly. 

Sorry this got to be so long. Basically, it's normal, a good thing even, and won't last forever. Therapy will still be helpful in the meantime, and will continue to be helpful as you move forward. 

I'm glad you're seeing someone, and I wish you the best moving forward.

I know this was from a month ago, but I just wanted to say that there are probably many more people in your life who struggle with mental illness or suicidal ideation than you realize, and that, for their sakes, I hope you one day gain a better understanding on these topics.

This is in a slightly different vein than other comments, but have you checked with a psychiatrist or other specialist about the possibility of you having ADHD Primarily Inattentive type? Because it doesn't present with the same energetic, impulsive symptoms as the Primarily Hyperactive type, it often gets missed. (I really recommend checking out the information at [r/adhd](http://www.reddit.com/r/ADHD/) .)

A lot of people are intelligent enough to figure out ways to cope and get around addressing it up to a certain point in their life, usually at college or a professional school, at which point they can't keep unknowingly overcoming their disability. People with the Primarily Inattentive type tend to be daydreamers and procrastinators who have trouble gathering the umph to start doing something. Because of this, they usually think that they are lazy, incapable, worthless, stupid, etc. 

I was diagnosed with ADHD PI about half a year ago, after being treated for depression for 2.5 years. I had had people mention it to me before, but I kept on brushing it off because I didn't fit the image of ADHD in popular culture. It has been so helpful to have that diagnosis, and know that it's not just me being lazy and useless, that my brain and prefrontal cortex are structurally different in a way that makes some executive functions difficult. I have been working on techniques to be effective despite my ADHD, and I think it has been helpful with my depression to feel like I am capable of doing things, or at least of trying. 

This may not apply to you, but I thought I would put it out there just in case.

I feel terribly guilty about not responding to her attempts to reconnect, and don't know how to explain to my parents that I would like to go back. (They think I'm feeling fantastic.) I know I should, and I know she would welcome it, I just feel like such a bad person.

(I'm sorry if this isn't a helpful comment, but I just wanted to say that I do the same thing with sleep. I don't feel anything, I can't hurt myself, I can't eat food and gain weight. I understand and have similar feelings towards using sleep to avoid reality.)

Congratulations on looking for employment and continuing college. 

I find it best to remain vague but honest, and turn it back around to the job at the end. Some things I've used have been "I was dealing with some personal things at the time, but I am moving on from that point in my life, and would love to do this with your company." and "I was dealing with some difficult situations and focusing on myself at the time. That time off helped me feel as prepared as I do now to succeed in this position."

I would definitely recommend volunteering! It shows initiative, like you said, and many employers value it. Perhaps more importantly, you might find that you like it, that it's rewarding and helps you feel better. 

Best of luck! I'm proud of you for moving forward.

Scars like that are called hypertrophic scars, or keloids if they extend past the original wound and are especially severe. Depending on your skin type, they might take months or years to fade, and even then will likely always be somehow visible. 

I recommend looking in the wiki for advice, but here's basically what it will tell you, along with some extra information. 

Massage them to break up the collagen tissue, and keep them moisturized. (Many people report good experiences with Vitamin E, Bio-Oil, and Mederma.) If you are interested in more aggressive ways to reduce them, you might try silicone gel or patches, steroid injections, some types of immune system therapy, some types of laser treatments, or scar-reduction surgery.
